title: 30 Months After Uproar Over Jonathan Glazer’s Oscar Speech, What Do His Pro-Israel Denouncers Say Now?
content:
By Norman Solomon*

SAN FRANCISCO, 15 October 2026 (IDN) — If you understand that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, why read an article focusing on the viewpoints of people who vehemently deny it? I wasn’t sure how to explain why, until I remembered something that screenwriter Frédéric Krivine said when I interviewed him in Paris eight years ago. He was the head scriptwriter of the brilliant film series Un Village Français, dramatizing the Nazi occupation of France during World War Two.

“People who do horrible things are human beings,” Krivine said. “We have to find a way to talk about them without hiding what they do and without treating them as nonhuman people, nonhuman beings. They are human beings; like us they belong to, we are in, the same species, human species…. It’s humans who kill now everywhere in the world where people are killed. It’s because they are human beings that we have problems – because if they were just extraterrestrial or monsters we could just erase them.”

title: UN Experts Warn FAO Against Sidelining Human Rights
content:
By Jaya Ramachandran

Independent UN experts say the right to food and international humanitarian law must remain central to FAO’s work, warning that staff should not face reprisals for documenting starvation and famine in Gaza.

GENEVA | 14 October 2026 (IDN) — A group of United Nations human rights experts has called on the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) to reaffirm human rights as a core part of its mandate and to ensure that staff can work on politically sensitive issues without fear of retaliation.

In a statement issued on 13 October, the experts expressed concern over recent remarks by FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu that, in their view, appeared to play down the role of human rights in the organisation’s work. They also raised questions about how FAO treated staff involved in examining violations of the right to food and international humanitarian law in Gaza.

“Human rights principles are not peripheral to the FAO’s mandate; they are central to it,” the experts said. They stressed that FAO and its management, as part of the UN system, are bound by the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect for human rights.

title: Brexit Will End and Europe Will Come Together Again
content:
By Jonathan Power

LUND, Sweden | 14 October 2026 (IDN) — At last, a British prime minister who is not afraid to say Europe is good for Britain. After a slow start on the issue, Andy Burnham has now made it fairly clear that Britain will seek to rejoin the European Union. It is not going to happen tomorrow, but it will surely not take 10 years to complete the entry negotiations, as some commentators are saying. Once completed, Britain will be able to go forward once again. It will be joining a success- a continent for thousands of years riven by war, but since 1945 has had no wars among its members. (Ex-Yugoslavia and Ukraine have never been members.)

The European Union is certainly not failing. In fact, it is about to get stronger. Adding the second-largest European economy will strengthen it. The British have learnt their lesson. So have the European Union members, albeit in a different way.

title: The International Year of Volunteerism: an Opportunity for a Profound Reset
content:
By Simone Galimberti*

KATHMANDU, Nepal 14 October 2026 (IDN)— A lost opportunity. I can’t find better words to describe the rollout of the International Year of Volunteerism 2026, a rare opportunity to embed and experience the best humanity can offer.

Volunteerism and civic engagement, the latter a broader concept that encompasses a variety of forms of active citizenship, are about positive values like solidarity, reciprocity, self-help, and generosity that, if applied, can truly make our world a better place.

Yet there is a gap between the potential of volunteerism and its perception across the globe, a real gulf between what volunteerism could contribute to and the importance attached to it by the people, institutions and society at large.

Volunteerism suffers from a chronic ailment that remains difficult to diagnose, but in its essence, if there is a way to explain it, I would call this illness “invisibility”.

Volunteers are not scarce; quite the opposite.

title: Why Shift Mental Halth Care from Institutions to Communities
content:
By Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus (WHO Director-General) and Anura Kumara Dissanayake (Sri Lanka President)

TIME first published this commentary on 12 October 2026, and it is reproduced with WHO’s permission.

GENEVA | 13 October 2026 (IDN) — In recent decades, many countries have made meaningful progress in developing community-based mental health services. Moreover, rights-based approaches have gained traction as people with lived experience increasingly have a voice in shaping mental health policy and services. These developments have shown that people living with mental health conditions can flourish in their communities when given the right support.

Yet, around the world, very large numbers of people with mental health conditions live behind closed doors in psychiatric hospitals and social care institutions. Some have been there for months; others for decades. According to the World Health Organization’s Mental Health Atlas, about half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear or when to eat, and cut off from the outside world.

title: A Nobel for Justice as Washington Moves Against the World Court
content:
Navi Pillay’s Peace Prize and sweeping US sanctions on the International Criminal Court place two opposing views of international law before the world.

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | THE HAGUE 13 October 2026 (IDN) — On the same day that the United States announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court as an institution, the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded its Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.

The coincidence could hardly have been more pointed. One decision honoured a jurist who has spent much of her life trying to hold perpetrators of grave crimes accountable. The other threatened the Court created to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes when national courts fail or refuse to act.

The Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 prize to the 85-year-old South African “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”. It said international law was under intense pressure and the institutions established to uphold it were being attacked.

Navi Pillay’s Peace Prize and sweeping US sanctions on the International Criminal Court place two opposing views of international law before the world.

title: UN and The Hague Confront Impunity for War Crimes
content:
By Nicolas J. S. Davies

NEW YORK | 12 October 2026 (IDN) — On 9 October 2026, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African international lawyer who defended Nelson Mandela and the anti-apartheid political prisoners on Robben Island, and went on to serve as a judge on the UN International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In 2025, Navi Pillay led the UN Commission of Inquiry that confirmed that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

With the world in the grip of seemingly intractable war and chaos, the Nobel Committee clearly wanted to honour someone who has worked against the tide of militarism and violence to uphold international law. Yet, on the same day, the United States unveiled unilateral, illegal coercive measures, or “sanctions”, against the ICC, where Navi Pillay served as a judge from 2003 to 2008.

The UN General Assembly’s 2026 general debate in September also set out to uphold the UN Charter and international law, and to confront the reality that the UN system is failing in its most basic responsibility, to maintain international peace and security.

title: A Cultural Turning Point for American Democracy
content:
What artists and religious leaders reveal about the health and future of democracy

By Azza Karam

NEW YORK, 12 OCTOBER 2026 (IDN) — A concert can tell us more about a country than an election poll can. It can reveal whose suffering people are prepared to acknowledge, what powerful institutions will permit them to say, and whether others will stand beside someone who pays a price for speaking.

In September, Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran’s American tour after expressing support for Palestinians onstage. Sheeran said the promoter decided against objections from stadium owners. Robert Kraft, whose company owns Gillette Stadium, defended excluding Macklemore, citing what he described as antisemitic rhetoric and imagery. Macklemore disputed that characterisation. Other supporting performers withdrew in solidarity—Reuters reporting and Associated Press reporting.

title: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push
content:
By Medea Benjamin

NEW YORK | 12 October 2026 (IDN) — For the third week in a row, high school students across France are taking to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.

But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people—or in missiles, weapons and war? Books or bombs?

What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On 6 October, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets to support the students.

title: Two African Wars Put Civilians—and the UN’s Authority—at Risk
content:
Ethiopia and Eritrea trade accusations before the Security Council as another deadly strike hits displaced families in Sudan.

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | ADDIS ABABA | KHARTOUM (IDN) — Wars in Ethiopia and Sudan are testing how far the United Nations can act when appeals for restraint are ignored.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have carried their rapidly escalating dispute to the Security Council. Farther west, a drone strike in Sudan’s Blue Nile state has killed dozens of displaced civilians, including women and children.

Although the conflicts have different origins, civilians in both countries are paying for failed agreements and delayed diplomacy.

Ethiopia told the Security Council that Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60 kilometres into its territory. It described the reported incursion as an “all-out invasion” and asserted its right to self-defence.

Eritrea denied the allegation and submitted its own letter to the Council. It accused Ethiopia of manufacturing a pretext for war. It asked for condemnation and “deterrent measures” under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which permits action ranging from sanctions to military force.

title: The Slow-Motion Erasure Of The West Bank
content:
By Dr Alon Ben-Meir*

A people are being erased not in a single cataclysm, but through daily terror: bulldozers, armed settlers, night raids, demolished homes, and stolen water. The West Bank’s suffering is not a security policy—it is a warning of Israel’s own moral collapse

NEW YORK | 10 October 2026 (IDN) — There are crimes that arrive with explosions, and crimes that advance quietly—through a bulldozer at dawn, a rifle at a shepherd’s chest, a child torn from bed, a family denied water until leaving becomes the only way to survive. In the West Bank, dispossession has become a daily ritual and Palestinian anguish a background noise too many have learned not to hear. Homes vanish, villages empty, children tremble through the night, and human beings are reduced to obstacles on land they have called home for generations. This is not security. It is ethnic cleansing, the deliberate destruction of a people’s ability to live.

title: Picasso’s Personal Mythologies: Three Paintings at the Currier Museum
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 9 October 2026 (IDN) — Manchester’s Currier Museum is currently presenting Personal Mythologies: Picasso in the 1940s and 50s—a small exhibition consisting of three paintings, two of which are on loan through October: L’Homme au béret basque (1946) and The Two Children (1954). The third, belonging to the Currier collection, is the remarkable Woman Seated in a Chair(1941), a portrait of the artist Dora Maar, painted in Picasso’s small Paris studio during the Nazi Occupation.

Maar was a French photographer, painter, and poet, and Picasso’s companion during those years. It is an extraordinarily vibrant painting, bold in its use of line and sharp geometric planes. What makes it truly devastating is hocsso’s brush transforms the simplest of themes—a seated woman—into a psychologically penetrating examination not of Maar or himself, but of their fraught relationship during a period of great uncertainty and immense social and political upheaval.

title: Germany’s Ukraine Policy: The Merz Factor
content:
By Wolfgang Bittner*

The following commentary reflects the author’s personal assessment of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s policy towards Ukraine.

GÖTTINGEN, Germany | 9 October 2026 (IDN) — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was pleased that Viktor Orbán was not re-elected and that the EU can transfer 90 billion euros to Ukraine. On 14 April 2026, he welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Berlin with military honours; among other things, they agreed on a “strategic partnership”. And on 4 October, he travelled to Kyiv for a solidarity visit, shortly after delivering an extremely anti-Russia speech on the occasion of the absurd awarding of the Peace of Westphalia Prize to NATO.
